title: Quirky but with a serious undertone?

commenti.body: Most of Jim Jarmusch’s work fits in this category. If I had to pick one to encapsulate it, would probably be Ghost Dog: Way of the Samurai. In general his movies never feel like they take place in our reality, and have wacky characters that do not behave like real people, but also always try to key into something that grounds it to the realism of the human experience.
Would you say this technique is similar to the [Distancing effect](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distancing_effect)?

A few films come to mind.

*Bad Fever* (2011; currently on the Criterion Channel) is, if you can imagine this, like a cringier, more depressing version of *The King of Comedy*.

I would also point to the films of Joel Potrykus, especially *Ape* and *Buzzard*, which have their moments of real humor but are for the most part awkward and somewhat uncomfortable to watch in a way that, at least in my opinion, really captures something about 21st century atomization and alienation.

Also *The Comedy* (2012) directed by Rick Alverson, which is very funny (if you like cringe comedy) but is also a somewhat unpleasant 94 minutes spent in the company of a coddled, terminally ironic manchild. I think it fits your description because it is -- or at least can be read -- as a rather vicious satire of the hipster subculture.

Have you seen any of these movies?
Probably Noah Baumbach's earlier works? Squid and the Whale comes to mind. It was weird seeing Jeff Daniels and Anna Paquin in a romantic role when I grew up with Fly Away Home, that's for sure.

I’d suggest Amelie. Definitely quirky, but deals with serious themes of isolation and making connections in modern times. Jeunet’s other movies, The City of Lost Children and Delicatessen might also fit but they’re a little less quirky and more sark and surreal

Speaking of French surrealism you could also look at The Science of Sleep by Michel Gondry

The first  Film that came to mind is *Everything is illuminated*, it might fit your description perfectly.

**Hunters in the Snow (2000)**

*A melancholic painter has an existential crisis triggered by the bulldozing of his local grocery store. There is an almost suffocating despair present throughout this movie, yet tinged with hope.*

**Tokyo Trash Baby**

*A lonely girl stalks her neighbour by collecting his trash. Low budget cinematography makes the subject matter uncomfortably voyeuristic.*

**Show Me Love (1998)**

*Two teenage girls deal with rumours about them being lesbians. Somehow avoiding ever becoming cheesy or exploitive, this movie is a sweet and charming story that fumbles along with its characters.*

**The Cement Garden**

*A teenage boy develops an unhealthy affection for his older sister. A fairly bleak look at life in the brutalist apartment blocks of England.*

**Hush! (2001)**

*An isolated and dysfunctional woman asks a gay man to be her sperm donor. All the characters in this movie are unhappy and reaching for connection, creating a series of unusual and uncomfortable situations.*

**God's Comedy**

*An eccentric ice cream maker sources his ingredients from some very strange and morally dubious places. This movie is simply bizarre and wholly unique.*

**Tamasha**

*Two people fed up with their lives cross paths on holiday, then have to deal with returning to humdrum reality. Idealistic and with some of the best montages I’ve seen. The characters have to decide whether or not to fight for their dreams or accept their mundane lives.*

**Palo Alto**

*Three teenagers struggle to find themselves in their privileged yet dysfunctional lives. Hazy and dreamlike, interwoven scenes of the lives of the characters.*

**God Help the Girl**

*A mentally ill girl finds salvation in music. A musical blending light drama with light comedy, it nevertheless has some dark moments.*

**Keiner Liebt Mich**

*A woman obsessed with death becomes close with her colourful neighbour who is full of life. The best movie to feature “La Vie en Rose” by Edith Piaf. A precious gem of a movie.*

Lily is the quiet, awkward loner who doesn’t fit in anywhere - but that could change.

Jarrod is a warrior in his own world who thinks he’s brave and powerful and is blind to Lily’s adoration – but that could change.

Lily crashes Jarrod’s party, ends up in his home town and lands a leading role in his hell bent plan to beat up an old high school bully.

They tackle estranged family, stranger friends only to find the real foe may be in the mirror.

The work of Aki Kaurismaki fits what you're looking for. Also:  
*Fish Story* (Yoshihiro Nakamura, 2009)  
*The Weather Man* (Gore Verbinski, 2005)  
*Wetlands* (David Wnendt, 2013)  
*Out of the Blue* (Dennis Hopper, 1980)
